summary: Documents tracing and non-blocking, or bypass, requirements for Open Pluggable Edge Services. Tracing lets endpoints learn which services touched their data, and bypass lets them avoid a service.

eli5.summary: If helpers change your parcel along the way, you should be able to see who touched it, and sometimes skip a helper. This document lists those needs.

questions: how do services identify themselves in opes
subtitle: How to trace and bypass services that transform data as it flows through the network.

tldr.problem: Network intermediaries can now transform application data (compress images, scan for viruses, adapt for mobile devices). Users and operators need to know which services touched their data and sometimes skip a broken service without losing access to content.
tldr.mechanism: OPES (Open Pluggable Edge Services) defines requirements for tracing—leaving a record of which services processed a message—and for bypass—allowing a user to request that a service be skipped if the original, unmodified content is available.
tldr.outcome: Systems can transparently adapt and transform data while remaining transparent and debuggable, and users can recover from service failures.

today: RFC 3897 is an Informational RFC published in September 2004. OPES architecture saw limited deployment; competing approaches to edge services became more common. The RFC remains a reference for understanding requirements for transparent intermediaries.

sections.title: Services That Transform Data
sections.content:
RFC 3897 documents tracing and bypass requirements for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES). OPES is an architecture that allows services running at the network edge—between a client and a server—to analyze and transform application messages. Examples include virus scanning, compression, format adaptation for mobile devices, and content filtering.

Two capabilities are essential for such a system. First, users and administrators must be able to see what services have processed their data, including which OPES systems were involved. Second, users must be able to request that a service be skipped if the original, unmodified version is available—important for recovering from a malfunctioning service without losing access entirely.
sections.eli5: Network services can change your data to make it smaller, safer, or better for your device. You need to know who changed it, and sometimes tell them to stop.

sections.title: OPES Systems, Entities, and Flows
sections.content:
An OPES System is the collection of all OPES entities authorized by either the data provider (the server) or data consumer (the client) to process a given message. An OPES System can include OPES processors (services that do the work), OPES services (what the processors offer), and callout servers (external helpers).

An OPES System is defined per message. An authorized entity does not necessarily process every message; some may sit idle for some requests. Two OPES Systems can process the same message simultaneously—one on the client side, one on the server side—but there can be no more than two.

An example is a Content Delivery Network (CDN) that uses OPES processors to adapt an image (resize it, reduce quality) before delivering it. The processors and services involved in those adaptations comprise an OPES System.
sections.eli5: An OPES System is a team of helpers authorized to transform your data. Each helper, and the service they offer, can be traced. Two teams can work on the same message (one at each end), but not more.

sections.title: Tracing Requirements
sections.content:
OPES trace is information about which OPES entities adapted a message. OPES tracing is the process of creating, manipulating, or interpreting that trace. Tracing is performed on a per-message basis and is embedded in the message itself (in-band).

An OPES System must add its entry to the trace. An OPES processor should add its entry. An OPES service may add its entry. Entities may delegate addition of their trace entry to another entity. At the system level, an entry must include the system's unique identification, information about its impact on data references, its privacy policy, and the party responsible for enforcing that policy. System entries should identify the processors involved.

The RFC compares a good trace to a trouble ticket: it is not necessarily a detailed description of what happened, but enough information for an operator to decode details and resolve problems. Administrators of different OPES Systems can have different ways of formatting and organizing trace information.
sections.eli5: Each helper signs the message saying they touched it. The signature includes who they are, what they did to the data, and where to find their privacy and safety rules. An operator can read these signatures to debug problems.

sections.title: Bypass (Skipping Services)
sections.content:
The bypass feature allows a user to instruct an OPES System to skip some or all of its services. A bypass request is an instruction containing a URI that identifies one or more OPES entities to skip.

To bypass a service means to not invoke it for that message. A bypass request is processed by each OPES processor in the flow; if non-OPES (unmodified) content is available, the processor bypasses the identified service and forwards the request to the next processor. Bypass requests are generally client-centric and go in the opposite direction of tracing.

If no non-OPES content is available without a specified service, the bypass request for that service is ignored. This design assumes most bypass requests are for situations where unmodified content is better than an error message. The bypass feature is comparable to an HTTP reload request to a cache—its purpose is to get usable content in the presence of failures, not to provide detailed information about what went wrong.
sections.eli5: A user can ask the helpers to skip one or two steps and give back the original. If that's not possible, they do the work anyway. It's like asking the laundry to send back your clothes unfolded because the folder is broken.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both tracing and bypass features present security risks. A compromised OPES entity can inject fake trace information—wrong service identifiers, excessively large traces that overflow buffers, or false claims of what happened to the data. Fake traces can be used to launch denial-of-service attacks or make debugging harder.

Non-OPES entities can also inject fake traces. OPES systems should verify that inserted traces come from legitimate entities, using authentication and authorization mechanisms. Policy can specify what trace information to expect from each peer.

The bypass feature can be abused by non-OPES entities or compromised OPES systems to bypass legitimate services—for example, skipping virus scanning or load balancing. A man-in-the-middle attacker can inject bypass instructions to knock out services, starve origin servers, or cause denial-of-service. Systems implementing access controls or logging via OPES can be misconfigured to honor bypass requests, giving unauthorized access or hiding traffic that should be monitored.

OPES entities should verify bypass instructions and check that they come from authorized sources. The RFC emphasizes that these are protocol-extension threats: proper implementation of authentication, authorization, and policy is essential.
sections.eli5: Bad actors can fake the signatures in traces to hide what they did, or inject fake bypass requests to skip important safety checks. The system needs to check that signatures are real and that bypass requests come from real users.
